name: Jamaican Beef Patties (Scotch Bonnet-Spiced Pastry)
type: Spiced Beef-Filled Pastry / Snack or Light Meal
imageAlt: Golden Jamaican beef patties split open to show their seasoned filling
imageCredit: Photo: ritcharnd moskow, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.
summary: Jamaican beef patties wrap a moist Scotch bonnet, thyme and allspice-seasoned filling in thin golden pastry that bakes crisp enough to scatter flakes with every bite.
lead: A good Jamaican patty is built on contrast: a brittle, unmistakably yellow crust around beef that stays finely textured, juicy and aromatic without leaking through the seam.
about: The Jamaican patty is a crescent-shaped pastry sold by bakeries, shops and street vendors across the island and carried widely through Jamaican migration. Beef is the best-known filling, though chicken, vegetable, seafood and other versions are established parts of the category. Its shell is thin, yellow from turmeric or Jamaican curry powder, and flaky from firm fat; the beef inside is not a dry crumble but a cohesive, spoonable mixture scented with scallion, thyme, allspice and Scotch bonnet. In Jamaica, a patty may be eaten alone or tucked into soft coco bread for a more substantial meal.
story: Jamaica's official tourism authority describes the patty as an island lunchtime favorite derived from the Cornish pasty introduced under British rule and transformed through Jamaican seasoning and technique. That concise history explains the form without treating the modern patty as merely imported: Scotch bonnet, thyme, scallion, allspice and the yellow crust give it a distinctly Jamaican identity. Jamaican cookbook authors Michelle and Suzanne Rousseau emphasize two present-day standards—the shell should shower flakes, while the beef should remain loose and gently stew-like rather than dense. Commercial patty shops made the portable pastry part of everyday island life, and diaspora bakeries carried it into cities far beyond Jamaica.
caveat: There is no single mandatory patty formula. Jamaican bakeries guard distinct doughs, spice blends, crimps and filling textures, and many use beef suet for a particularly crisp crust. This home version combines butter and shortening for reliable handling; replacing both with suet changes flavor and texture but is also documented. Scotch bonnets vary sharply in heat, so wear gloves, avoid touching your face and begin with half a seeded chile if needed. Cool the filling completely before assembly, keep the dough cold, and refrigerate cooked patties within 2 hours.
prepNotes: Visible pieces of cold butter and shortening create the flaky shell. If the dough becomes glossy or soft while rolling, chill it for 15 minutes before continuing.
The beef should be moist enough to spread but leave no liquid trail when a spoon crosses the skillet. Warm filling melts the pastry fat and makes weak, leaking seams.
Cool a teaspoon of filling before judging salt and chile. The flavor should be slightly more assertive than a plated stew because the pastry will soften its impact.
ingredients: 3 cups all-purpose flour, plus more for rolling
1/2 cup cold unsalted butter, cut into 1/2-inch cubes
1/2 cup cold vegetable shortening, cut into small pieces
2/3 cup ice water, plus up to 2 tbsp as needed
1 large egg beaten with 1 tbsp water, for egg wash
1 1/4 lb ground beef, preferably 85 percent lean
1 small yellow onion, very finely chopped
3 scallions, white and green parts finely chopped
1/2 to 1 Scotch bonnet chile, seeded and minced with gloves
1 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
steps: Whisk the flour, 1 tablespoon curry powder, turmeric, baking powder and 1 teaspoon salt in a wide bowl. Add the cold butter and shortening and cut them in with a pastry blender or fingertips until most pieces are pea-size and a few remain slightly larger.

Drizzle in 2/3 cup ice water while tossing with a fork. Squeeze a handful: it should hold together without feeling wet. Add more ice water 1 tablespoon at a time only if dry flour remains, then press the shaggy dough into a disk without kneading it smooth.

Wrap the dough and refrigerate at least 1 hour. Checkpoint: before rolling, it should feel firm and cool but yield slightly when pressed; a rock-hard disk will crack, while a soft one will lose its flakes.

Heat the neutral oil in a wide skillet over medium-high. Add the beef and cook 5 to 7 minutes, breaking it into very fine pieces, until no pink remains and the released liquid has mostly evaporated. Drain only if more than 2 tablespoons of fat pool in the pan.

Add the onion, scallions, garlic, Scotch bonnet and thyme. Cook over medium heat 6 to 8 minutes, stirring, until the onion is soft and the sharp raw-chile aroma has mellowed. Stir in the allspice, black pepper, remaining curry powder and 1 teaspoon salt for 30 seconds.

Pour in the stock and optional browning sauce. Simmer uncovered 12 to 18 minutes, stirring and crushing the beef, until the mixture is moist but no broth pools when dragged aside. Stir in the breadcrumbs and cook 2 minutes; the filling should spread like a thick paste while retaining fine pieces of beef.
Transfer the filling to a shallow pan and cool uncovered for 20 minutes, then refrigerate until cold, at least 30 minutes. Taste a cooled spoonful and adjust salt or chile before assembling.

Line two baking sheets with parchment. Divide the dough into 10 equal pieces, keeping all but one refrigerated. On a lightly floured surface, roll each piece into a 6 1/2-inch round about 1/8 inch thick; trim around a bowl if a neater edge is desired.

Place a scant 1/3 cup cold filling just off-center on each round, leaving a 1/2-inch clean border. Brush the border lightly with cold water, fold into a half-moon and press out trapped air before sealing. Crimp firmly with a fork without piercing the filled center.

Arrange the patties 1 inch apart on the sheets and chill 20 minutes. Meanwhile heat the oven to 375°F with racks in the upper and lower thirds. Checkpoint: the patties should feel cold and the edges should remain tightly sealed before baking.

Brush lightly with egg wash and cut one small steam slit in each top. Bake 28 to 35 minutes, rotating and switching the sheets halfway, until the crust is dry, crisp and deep golden at the edges and the centers register at least 165°F.

Cool 8 to 10 minutes before eating; the filling will be dangerously hot straight from the oven. Serve on their own or inside coco bread. Refrigerate leftovers up to 3 days and reheat at 350°F until the crust is crisp and the center is steaming.

name: Nigerian Beef Suya (Yaji-Spiced Skewers)
region: Northern Nigeria and cities across Nigeria / Hausa foodways
type: Spiced Grilled Beef Skewers / Street Food
imageAlt: Assorted Nigerian suya skewers of beef, chicken and gizzard arranged on a platter
summary: Nigerian beef suya threads paper-thin sirloin onto skewers, seasons it with aromatic basic yaji, grills it over fierce heat and serves it with nutty yajin kuli, onion and tomato.
lead: Suya should taste of smoke, chile, ginger and beef before the groundnut-rich serving spice arrives—the distinction between grilling yaji and yajin kuli keeps the coating fragrant instead of scorched.
about: Suya is thinly sliced meat threaded on skewers, seasoned and roasted over live coals. Its craft is rooted in Hausa foodways of northern Nigeria and is now a defining evening street food in Lagos and cities across the country. Beef is classic, while ram, chicken, gizzard and offal versions are also sold. Nigerian food historian Ozoz Sokoh distinguishes the nut-free basic yaji used on meat before grilling from yajin kuli, the groundnut-rich spice offered after cooking. This recipe keeps that distinction and uses unsweetened defatted peanut powder as the practical home analogue for ground kuli-kuli.
story: Pan-Atlantic University's Centenary Project documents suya as a Hausa specialty that became one of Nigeria's most visible street foods, prepared by skilled vendors and shared from paper parcels with sliced onion and tomato. The grill is part of the social scene as well as the cooking method: skewers are selected, reheated, cut into bites and dusted to order. Sokoh's research also records how incomplete views of vendor preparation led many diaspora recipes to put peanut-rich yajin kuli on the raw meat. Her later work with northern Nigerian cooks clarified that basic yaji seasons the grill, while fresh yajin kuli is the finishing spice. This home method follows that division without pretending a domestic grill reproduces a mai suya's practiced charcoal fire.
caveat: Yaji recipes are vendor and household knowledge, so spice proportions, meat cuts and serving garnishes legitimately vary. Suya and yajin kuli commonly contain groundnut and are unsafe for anyone with a peanut allergy; omitting the peanut powder makes a different finishing blend, so do not present it as equivalent. Slice intact beef against the grain, refrigerate it while marinating and cook to at least 145°F followed by a 3-minute rest. Soak wooden skewers, grill outdoors with good ventilation and never use newspaper as food wrapping because printing inks are not intended for food contact.
prepNotes: Twenty to thirty minutes in the freezer makes sirloin steady enough to cut across the grain into even 1/8-inch ribbons that cook before the spice burns.
Basic yaji goes on the raw beef. Peanut-rich yajin kuli is reserved for the cooked skewers and table; its fine groundnut solids scorch over direct heat.
A very hot side creates quick char, while a cooler side lets you finish any thicker folds without blackening the ginger and chile coating.
ingredients: 1 1/2 lb beef sirloin or blade steak, trimmed of silverskin
3 tbsp neutral oil, plus more for the grill grate
12 bamboo skewers, soaked in water for at least 30 minutes
1 to 2 tsp cayenne pepper, to taste
1/2 tsp finely ground black pepper or African cubeb pepper
1/2 tsp ground grains of Selim, optional
1/2 cup plain unsweetened defatted peanut powder
1/2 tsp additional cayenne pepper, or to taste
1 medium red onion, very thinly sliced
steps: Wrap the trimmed beef and freeze it for 20 to 30 minutes, until firm at the edges but not frozen solid. With a sharp knife, slice across the grain into strips about 2 inches long, 1 inch wide and 1/8 inch thick.

For the basic yaji, mix 1 tablespoon ginger, 2 teaspoons paprika, onion powder, garlic powder, 1 to 2 teaspoons cayenne, 1 1/2 teaspoons salt, black or cubeb pepper, optional grains of Selim and cloves. Measure 3 tablespoons into a small cup for seasoning the meat; reserve any extra in a clean jar.

For the yajin kuli, whisk the peanut powder with the additional 1 teaspoon ginger, 1 teaspoon paprika, 1/2 teaspoon cayenne and 1/2 teaspoon salt. It should be loose and sandy, not oily or clumped. Set it far from the raw-beef work area so it remains safe for serving.

Toss the beef with the neutral oil, then sprinkle over the measured basic yaji in two additions, massaging gently until every surface is evenly rust-red. Cover and refrigerate 30 minutes and up to 8 hours.

Thread each strip through twice so it lies flat rather than bunching, leaving 2 inches bare at each end of the skewer. Arrange the completed skewers on a clean tray and refrigerate while heating the grill.

Prepare a charcoal or gas grill for two-zone high heat, about 450°F at the grate. Clean and oil the grate. Checkpoint: the hot zone should sear a test edge of beef immediately without tall flames; move or spread coals if grease causes flare-ups.
Lay the skewers over direct heat in a single uncrowded layer. Grill 3 to 4 minutes, until the underside is deeply browned in spots and releases from the grate, then turn and cook 3 to 4 minutes more.

Check the thickest folded piece with an instant-read thermometer. It should reach at least 145°F; move any underdone skewers to the cooler zone, cover and cook 1 to 3 minutes more without burning the spice.

Transfer to a clean platter and rest 3 minutes. While the surface is still warm, dust the skewers lightly with yajin kuli, keeping most of the blend in a separate serving bowl so each diner can control heat and nuttiness.
Serve immediately with sliced red onion, tomato and optional cucumber. Label the platter clearly for peanut allergy and provide clean tongs rather than returning any utensil that touched raw beef.

Refrigerate leftover cooked beef within 2 hours for up to 3 days. Reheat briefly under a hot broiler or on a grill just until steaming; prolonged reheating makes the thin slices leathery. Discard serving spice contaminated by meat or used utensils.

name: Bengali Shorshe Ilish (Hilsa in Mustard Sauce)
region: Bangladesh and the Bengal region / Bengali foodways
category: Hilsa fish in fresh mustard sauce
imageAlt: Homemade Bengali shorshe ilish with hilsa steaks in golden mustard gravy and green chiles
imageCredit: Photo: Sm faysal, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.
summary: Bengali shorshe ilish gently cooks rich bone-in hilsa steaks in a pungent sauce of freshly ground yellow and black mustard, green chile, turmeric and mustard oil.
lead: Shorshe ilish is an exercise in restraint: oily hilsa, fresh mustard, green chile and turmeric need little else, but the mustard must be ground cool and the fragile fish barely handled.
about: Shorshe ilish means mustard hilsa. The dish belongs across Bengal, with particular prominence in Bangladesh, where ilish is the national fish and an important source of food, livelihood and cultural memory. Bone-in hilsa steaks are coated with turmeric and salt, then cooked gently in fresh mustard paste, green chile and mustard oil. The sauce should remain bright, pungent and fluid enough to run through plain rice. This version does not fry the steaks first, preserving the especially soft texture and allowing the fish's own abundant oil to enrich the mustard gravy.
story: Hilsa migrates between the Bay of Bengal and the region's rivers, linking the dish to monsoon seasons, fishing communities and the ecology of the Padma, Meghna, Ganges and Hooghly systems. Bangladesh's Department of Fisheries identifies ilish as the national fish and manages sanctuaries, juvenile-catch restrictions and seasonal protections, while WorldFish describes it as present in the country's markets, poetry, history and dinner tables. Shorshe ilish is one celebrated expression of that relationship, but not the only one: hilsa is fried, steamed, wrapped in leaves and cooked with several regional sauces. Mustard-ilish preparations also vary between Bangladeshi and Indian Bengali households in seed ratios, frying, poppy seed, yogurt and the thickness of the gravy.
caveat: Hilsa contains many fine forked bones and must be eaten slowly and attentively; warn every diner and do not serve bone-in pieces to young children or anyone unable to manage them safely. Buy mature, legally harvested hilsa from a reputable source and respect current local fishery restrictions—juvenile jatka should not be purchased. Use only mustard oil explicitly sold for culinary use in your jurisdiction, never a cosmetic or external-use product. Mackerel is an oily practical substitute, but the result is mustard fish, not shorshe ilish, and should be named accordingly.
prepNotes: Soak the seeds, use cool water and pulse rather than running the blender continuously. Excess heat and damaged hulls can make the paste harshly bitter.
All hilsa steaks should fit in one layer. Stacking or repeated turning breaks the delicate fish and makes the fine bones harder to navigate.
Frozen mature hilsa from a reputable Bengali or Bangladeshi grocer is preferable to illegally caught juvenile fish. Thaw overnight in the refrigerator and pat dry gently.
ingredients: 1 1/2 lb bone-in hilsa steaks, about 6 pieces, thawed if frozen
1 1/2 tsp fine sea salt, divided, plus more to taste
1 tbsp black or brown mustard seeds
3/4 cup warm water, plus cool water for soaking and grinding
Steamed short- or medium-grain white rice, for serving
steps: Put the yellow and black mustard seeds in a small bowl, cover with cool water and soak 30 minutes. Drain thoroughly. Keep the water and blender jar cool rather than warm so friction does not turn the paste bitter.
Pat the hilsa steaks dry without pulling at the flesh. Rub them gently with 1/2 teaspoon turmeric and 1/2 teaspoon salt and set aside for 15 minutes while making the paste.

Blend the drained mustard seeds with 2 green chiles, 1/2 teaspoon salt and 3 tablespoons cool water in short pulses. Scrape the jar and add water 1 teaspoon at a time until the paste is smooth and pourable, never letting the jar become hot.

Taste only a tiny dab of the mustard paste. It should be powerfully pungent but not acrid. For an especially smooth sauce, push it through a fine sieve and discard the coarse hulls rather than continuing to grind them.
Heat 4 tablespoons culinary mustard oil in a wide lidded skillet over medium until shimmering. If using nigella, add it and cook 20 to 30 seconds, just until fragrant; do not let the seeds blacken.

Lower the heat. Stir in the mustard paste, remaining 1/2 teaspoon turmeric and 3/4 cup warm water. Add 1/2 teaspoon salt and 2 slit green chiles, then bring only to a gentle simmer for 3 minutes. The raw edge should soften while the sauce stays yellow and fluid.
Slide the hilsa steaks into the sauce in one layer and spoon gravy over their tops. Cover and cook over low heat for 5 minutes, keeping the sauce at a lazy simmer rather than a hard boil.

Turn each steak once with a thin spatula and support it with a spoon. Cover and cook 4 to 6 minutes more. Checkpoint: the flesh should be opaque and moist, separate at the outer edge under gentle pressure and register 145°F at the thickest part.

Remove the pan from the heat. Add the remaining green chile, slit lengthwise, and drizzle over the final 1 tablespoon culinary mustard oil. Cover and rest 5 minutes so the sharp aroma settles into the sauce without further cooking the fish.
Taste the gravy around the fish and adjust salt with a light hand. Serve one steak per diner with plenty of hot rice and explain the fine bones before anyone begins eating.

Cool leftovers within 2 hours and refrigerate in a shallow covered container for no more than 1 day. Reheat once, covered and very gently, adding a spoonful of water so the sauce loosens without breaking the fish.
